Chapter 24

Storage: pushdown, and the rule for when not to

Compiling a predicate to SQL when — and only when — SQL’s answer is identical, including nulls.

By the end of this chapter

Make queries fast without ever making them different.

The evaluator can answer any query. The database can answer some of them much faster. The whole of this file is one question: which ones, and how do you stay honest about it?

The rule

null from compile is not a failure — it means "the evaluator will do this one", which is always correct and sometimes slower. Returning something *approximate* would be faster and wrong, in the way that is hardest to notice: a filter that returns nearly the right rows.

The specific case worth knowing is attributes.status >= 500. SQLite has json_extract, so it looks pushable. It is not: SQLite compares an extracted value as text, and the evaluator compares a numeric string numerically, so the two would silently return different rows.

Stop at the first predicate you cannot push

Skipping an unpushable predicate and continuing is the tempting version and it is wrong. A summarize in the middle changes what the columns *mean*, so a where after it refers to computed columns that do not exist in the table. Pushing a later filter because an earlier one was pushable applies it to the wrong thing.

The classic pushdown bug

If the evaluator still has filtering to do, the database’s idea of "the first 100" is the first 100 of a *larger* set. Taking them at the database is the classic mistake: a LIMIT moved above a filter, producing a page of results that is stable, plausible and missing rows.

And a projection, added because a test found what was missing

The first version used db.select() with no projection. That returns every column — including id, tenant_id and received_at — and keys them by Drizzle’s JavaScript names, so a row arrived with traceId while SQF calls the column trace_id.

Both halves were bugs and both were invisible from inside. Internal columns reached the results table, and the chart view — which picks the first numeric column — found id and drew a beautiful straight line of primary keys. Worse, a predicate on trace_id worked when it was pushed to SQL and matched nothing when it fell back to the evaluator, so the answer depended on whether the planner happened to push it.

Testing a planner the same way we tested the evaluator

The oracle loads every row in the window and runs only the evaluator. A disagreement is *always* a pushdown bug, because the oracle has nothing to be wrong about. That is the same technique as chapter 14, applied one layer down, and it is how the two projection bugs above got their regression tests.

Checkpoint

  • A pushed query and an evaluator-only query return identical rows, nulls included.
  • A take after an unpushable filter is applied by the evaluator, not by SQL.
  • from logs returns only the columns the schema documents.
